newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai foreign bond issues stalled, await Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Thai foreign bond issues stalled, await Moody's.

text.p: Thailand is unlikely to issue any new debt instruments in international markets until Moody's Investors Service makes a final decision on whether to downgrade the country's sovereign debt rating, analysts said on Thursday.
The ratings agency last month unnerved markets when it placed Thailand's A2 foreign-currency sovereign ceilings for bonds and bank deposits under review for a possible downgrade.
Since then, Moody's officials have visited Thailand to gather economic data in advance of a final decision, expected in about two months.
Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said earlier this month that he had postponed a U.S. roadshow to promote Thailand's planned launch of $500 million in Yankee bonds.
He said he had delayed the trip until April to focus on the country's battered financial sector and problems related to a four-year slump in the domestic property sector.
Analysts saw the delay as also linked to the Moody's review.

"Even the government itself decided that the market is too volatile to launch the (bond) issue. It's quite natural that other issues would have similar thinking," said Toni Li, managing director of primary markets at Chase Manahattan Asia.
"If Moody's put another country on the credit watch, I think a similar reaction will be seen in the market place," he told Reuters.
Most Thai issuers had put new issues on hold because of concerns about foreign investor demand and high interest costs, analysts said.

"Most plans have been delayed, which is the best thing they can do now," said one syndicate banker at a Singapore-based European bank. "It's a wait-and-see type of position. It's no panic, just hang in there."
Siam City Bank Plc has halted its plan to launch $100 million in floating-rate certificates of deposit due partly to Moody's possible downgrade.
The issue was scheduled to be completed last month.
"Siam City Bank (officials) think they have other funding sources, they don't want to come to the market and pay the market price," said Li at Chase Manhattan, the lead arranger for the issue.
Analysts expect any downgrade of Thailand's credit ratings to raise borrowing costs abroad for Thai firms.

"We must accept the country's economic condition during this time. The possible downgrade would have some pressure on the cost of foreign borrowings," said Anothai Techamontrikul, senior vice president of Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand.
The Bank of Thailand projects 1997 gross domestic product growth at 6.8 percent compared with 6.7 a year ago, but private economists expected lower growth this year.
